A1: cos 3θ = cos³θ − 3 cos θ sin²θ
A1: sin 3θ = 3 cos²θ sin θ − sin³θ

long.q: Find the five roots of z⁵ = 1 in the form e^(iθ). By considering the sum of the roots, show that cos(2π/5) + cos(4π/5) = −½.

A1: integrating factor e^(∫2/x dx) = x²

B1: e^(−2x) → 0, so y → 2 (oscillations die away)

B1: e^(2x) is in the CF, so the trial particular integral is kx e^(2x)
M1: substitute: y′ = k(1 + 2x)e^(2x), y″ = k(4 + 4x)e^(2x), giving 5k = 10

long.q: Use the substitution y = vx to solve dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), for x > 0, given that y = 2 when x = 1. Give y² in terms of x.
scheme: M1: dy/dx = v + x dv/dx substituted
A1: v + x dv/dx = 1/v + v, so x dv/dx = 1/v
M1: separate variables and integrate: ∫ v dv = ∫ 1/x dx
M1: use y = 2, x = 1 (v = 2) to find c = 2

questions.why: No horizontal force acts.

questions.q: A particle is projected from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², what is its time of flight?
questions.why: The vertical component is 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹; the time of flight is 2 × 10/10 = 2 s. Using cos 30° gives 3.46 s.

questions.q: A particle is projected at 10 m s⁻¹ at 45° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², what is the equation of its trajectory?
questions.why: y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u²cos²θ) = x − 10x²/(2 × 100 × ½) = x − x²/10.

long.q: A particle is projected from a point O on horizontal ground with speed 25 m s⁻¹ at an angle θ above the horizontal, where tan θ = 3/4. Show that the equation of its trajectory is y = 3x/4 − x²/80, where x and y are the horizontal and vertical displacements in metres from O. Find the horizontal distance from O of the particle when it is 10 m above the ground and descending. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: x = 25 cos θ t = 20t and y = 25 sin θ t − 5t² = 15t − 5t²
M1: eliminate t using t = x/20
A1: x = 40 m (x = 20 is on the way up)

long.q: A particle is projected from O with speed 20 m s⁻¹ at an angle α above the horizontal, and passes through the point 20 m horizontally and 5 m vertically above O. Find the two possible values of α. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: use the trajectory y = x tan α − gx²(1 + tan²α)/(2V²) with x = 20, y = 5
A1: 5 = 20 tan α − 5(1 + tan²α), giving tan²α − 4 tan α + 2 = 0
M1: solve the quadratic in tan α

long.q: A particle is projected with speed 30 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal. Find the time after projection at which the particle is moving at 45° below the horizontal, and its speed at that instant. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: horizontal component of velocity stays 30 cos 60° = 15 m s⁻¹
M1: vertical component 30 sin 60° − 10t = −15 when moving at 45° below the horizontal

long.q: A stone is thrown from a point 40 m above horizontal ground with speed 15 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Find the time taken for the stone to reach the ground, the horizontal distance travelled, and its speed on hitting the ground. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: use energy (v² = 15² + 2 × 10 × 40) or combine velocity components

long.q: A particle is projected from a point on horizontal ground with speed V at an angle θ above the horizontal. Show that its range on the ground is V² sin 2θ/g. Given that V = 14 m s⁻¹, state the maximum possible range and find the two angles of projection that give a range of 15 m. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: time of flight from V sin θ t − ½gt² = 0: t = 2V sin θ/g
M1: range = V cos θ × 2V sin θ/g
A1: = V² sin 2θ/g using 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ

Only the resultant force is zero

questions.q: A uniform rod AB, 2 m long and of weight 40 N, rests horizontally on supports at A and at C, where AC = 1.5 m. What is the reaction at C?
questions.why: Moments about A: R_C × 1.5 = 40 × 1, so R_C = 80/3 ≈ 26.7 N (and R_A = 13.3 N).

questions.q: A uniform cube of side 0.4 m and weight W rests on rough horizontal ground. A horizontal force P acts at the middle of a top edge, perpendicular to a face. If the cube does not slide, at what value of P is it about to topple?
questions.why: On the point of toppling it pivots on the far lower edge: P × 0.4 = W × 0.2, so P = W/2. It topples before sliding only if μ > 1/2.

long.q: A uniform ladder of length 2a and weight W rests with its upper end against a smooth vertical wall and its lower end on rough horizontal ground, where the coefficient of friction is 0.4. The ladder is about to slip when it makes an angle θ with the horizontal. Find θ.
scheme: B1: resolving vertically, normal reaction at the ground R = W
M1: moments about the foot: S × 2a sin θ = W × a cos θ, where S is the wall reaction
M1: resolving horizontally F = S, with limiting friction F = 0.4R

long.q: A uniform square lamina ABCD has side 10 cm. A square of side 4 cm, with one corner at C and sides along CB and CD, is removed. Find the distances of the centre of mass of the remaining lamina from AB and from AD. The remaining lamina is freely suspended from B and hangs in equilibrium. Find the angle that BA makes with the vertical.
scheme: M1: moments using areas 100, 16 and 84 with centres 5 cm and 8 cm from AD (and from AB)
A1: distance from AB = 31/7 cm (by symmetry)
M1: when suspended from B, BG is vertical

long.q: A uniform rectangular block of weight 50 N, with height 0.6 m and square base of side 0.4 m, rests on rough horizontal ground with coefficient of friction 0.5. A horizontal force P N is applied at the midpoint of a top edge, perpendicular to that edge, and is gradually increased. Determine whether the block slides or topples first.
scheme: M1: on the point of toppling, take moments about the lower edge: P × 0.6 = 50 × 0.2
M1: on the point of sliding, P = F = μR = 0.5 × 50
A1: 16.7 < 25, so the block topples first

long.q: A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and weight 40 N is freely hinged to a vertical wall at A and held horizontal by a light string from B to a point C on the wall 1.5 m vertically above A. Find the tension in the string and the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the hinge on the rod.
scheme: M1: moments about A: T sin α × 2 = 40 × 1, with sin α = 0.6 (α = angle between string and rod)
M1: resolve horizontally and vertically for the hinge force components
A1: horizontal 80/3 N away from the wall, vertical 40 − 20 = 20 N upwards
long.ans: T = 33.3 N; hinge force 33.3 N at 36.9° above the horizontal

long.q: A uniform solid consists of a cylinder of radius r and height 2r with a hemisphere of radius r joined to one end so that their plane faces coincide. M1: on the point of toppling, G is vertically above the lowest point of the base: tan α = r ÷ x̄

questions.q: A particle on a light inextensible string of length 1 m moves in a vertical circle. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², what is the least speed at the lowest point for it to complete the circle?
questions.why: At the top the tension can just be zero, so v² = gl = 10. Energy: u² = v² + 2g(2l) = 10 + 40 = 50. (√40 would be enough for a rod, not a string.)

long.q: A car travels round a bend of radius 80 m on a road banked at 15° to the horizontal. Find the speed at which there is no tendency to slip. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.3. Find the greatest speed at which the car can travel round the bend without slipping. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]

M1: at maximum speed friction μR acts down the slope; resolve vertically and horizontally
M1: eliminate R: v² = 800(sin 15° + 0.3 cos 15°)/(cos 15° − 0.3 sin 15°)

long.q: A particle of mass 0.3 kg is attached to a light inextensible string of length 0.8 m whose other end is fixed at O. The particle moves in a vertical circle with centre O and has speed 7 m s⁻¹ at its lowest point. Find the tension in the string when the particle is at its highest point. Find also the least speed at the lowest point for which the particle completes the circle. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]

M1: for completion T ≥ 0 at the top, so v² ≥ gl = 8 and u² ≥ 8 + 32

long.q: A particle is placed at the top of a smooth fixed sphere of radius 1.2 m and slightly displaced so that it slides down the outer surface from rest. Find the angle between the radius to the particle and the upward vertical when the particle leaves the surface, and its speed at that moment. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]

M1: leaves the surface when R = 0
A1: v² = ga cos θ = 8, v = 2.83 m s⁻¹

questions.q: What is the elastic potential energy stored in an elastic spring of natural length L and modulus of elasticity λ when extended by x?

questions.q: A particle hangs in equilibrium on an elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus 20 N, which is extended by 0.2 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², what is the mass of the particle?
questions.why: T = λx/l = 20 × 0.2/0.8 = 5 N; in equilibrium T = mg, so m = 5/10 = 0.5 kg.

long.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg hangs in equilibrium at the end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N, whose other end is fixed. Find the extension. The particle is pulled down a further 0.15 m and released from rest. Find its speed as it passes through the equilibrium position. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: elastic energy λx²/(2l) at extensions 0.35 m and 0.2 m: 1.53125 J and 0.5 J
M1: energy equation: loss of EPE = gain of GPE (0.5 × 10 × 0.15) + gain of KE

long.q: A particle of mass 2 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1.5 m and modulus of elasticity 60 N. The other end is attached to a fixed point O, and the particle is released from rest at O. Find the greatest extension of the string and the greatest distance of the particle below O. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: elastic energy at extension x is 60x²/(2 × 1.5) = 20x²
M1: loss of GPE = gain of EPE at the lowest point: 20(1.5 + x) = 20x²
B1: greatest distance below O = 3.32 m

long.q: A particle P lies on a smooth horizontal table between two fixed points A and B, which are 3 m apart. P is attached to A by a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus 20 N, and to B by a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus 30 N. Find the distance AP when P is in equilibrium, and the tension in each string.
scheme: M1: tensions T_A = 20(d − 1) and T_B = 30(2 − d), where AP = d
M1: in equilibrium the tensions are equal
A1: tension 12 N in each string

long.q: A particle of mass 0.4 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 0.6 m and modulus 12 N; the other end is fixed at A on a rough horizontal surface, with coefficient of friction 0.25. The particle is released from rest on the surface with AP = 0.9 m. Find the speed of the particle when the string first becomes slack. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: initial elastic energy λx²/(2l) with x = 0.3

long.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg is on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal, attached to a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus 10 N whose other end is fixed to a point on the plane higher up the line of greatest slope. Find the extension when the particle rests in equilibrium. The particle is then held with the string just taut and released from rest. Find the greatest extension in the subsequent motion. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]
scheme: M1: resolve along the plane: 10e/1 = 0.5 × 10 sin 30°
M1: energy: loss of GPE mgx sin 30° = gain of EPE λx²/(2l)

questions.why: 2v dv/dx = −4x, so v dv/dx = −2x and v² = 9 − 2x²; at x = 1, v² = 7. Forgetting to divide by the mass gives √5.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg particle starts from rest and is acted on by a force 6t N in its direction of motion. What is its speed when t = 2 s?
questions.why: a = F/m = 12t, so v = ∫ 12t dt = 6t² (v = 0 at t = 0); at t = 2, v = 24 m s⁻¹.

long.q: A car of mass 800 kg moves along a straight horizontal road with its engine working at a constant power of 16 kW. Resistances to motion are negligible. Find the distance travelled and the time taken while the speed increases from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹.
scheme: M1: Newton's second law with acceleration v dv/dx: 800v dv/dx = 16 000/v
M1: with acceleration dv/dt: 800v dv = 16 000 dt

long.q: A particle of mass 0.5 kg moves along the positive x-axis under a single force of magnitude 4/(x + 1)² N directed away from the origin O. It starts from rest at O. Find v² in terms of x, the speed when x = 3, and the speed that the particle approaches as x becomes large.
scheme: M1: Newton's second law with acceleration v dv/dx: 0.5v dv/dx = 4/(x + 1)²
M1: integrate: ¼v² = −4/(x + 1) + c, with v = 0 at x = 0 giving c = 4
A1: v = √12 = 3.46 m s⁻¹ when x = 3
B1: v approaches 4 m s⁻¹ as x → ∞

long.q: A particle of mass 0.2 kg moves in a horizontal straight line against a resistance of magnitude 0.05v² N, where v m s⁻¹ is its speed; no other horizontal force acts. Its speed falls from 20 m s⁻¹ to 5 m s⁻¹. Find the distance travelled and the time taken.

A particle of mass 3 kg starts from rest and moves in a straight line under a force (6t − t²) N in the direction of motion, where t is the time in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Find the greatest speed of the particle and the distance travelled in the 6 seconds.
scheme: M1: a = (6t − t²)/3 integrated with respect to t
A1: v = t² − t³/9 (v = 0 at t = 0)
M1: greatest speed when a = 0, i.e. t = 6
M1: integrate v to find x

long.q: A particle of mass 0.1 kg falls vertically from rest under gravity, against air resistance of magnitude 0.02v N, where v m s⁻¹ is its speed. Find v in terms of t, state its terminal speed, and find the time taken to reach half the terminal speed. [Take g = 10 m s⁻²]

o: The component parallel to the wall
The component perpendicular to the wall

questions.q: A smooth sphere hits a smooth fixed wall at 10 m s⁻¹, its velocity making 60° with the wall. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. What is its speed after impact?
questions.why: Parallel component 10 cos 60° = 5 is unchanged; normal component 10 sin 60° = 8.66 becomes 4.33. Speed = √(5² + 4.33²) ≈ 6.61 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Smooth sphere A, speed u, hits an identical sphere B at rest. A's velocity makes 30° with the line of centres and the collision is perfectly elastic (e = 1). How does A move afterwards?
o: It continues at speed u at 30° to the line of centres
Perpendicular to the line of centres, with speed u/2
Along the line of centres, with speed u/2
questions.why: Along the line of centres, equal masses with e = 1 exchange velocities, so A keeps only its perpendicular component u sin 30° = u/2.

long.q: A small smooth sphere moving on a smooth horizontal surface with speed 8 m s⁻¹ strikes a fixed smooth vertical wall. Its direction of motion makes an angle of 60° with the wall, and the coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find the speed of the sphere after the impact and the angle its new direction makes with the wall.
scheme: B1: component parallel to the wall unchanged: 8 cos 60° = 4 m s⁻¹
M1: component perpendicular to the wall multiplied by e: 0.5 × 8 sin 60°
A1: angle with the wall = tan⁻¹(2√3/4) = 40.9°

long.q: Two smooth spheres A and B of equal radius, with masses 2m and m, lie on a smooth horizontal surface. B is at rest. A moves with speed 5 m s⁻¹ and strikes B; at the instant of impact A's direction of motion makes an angle of 30° with the line of centres. The coefficient of restitution is ½. Find the speed of B after the collision, and the speed and direction of A after the collision.
scheme: B1: B moves along the line of centres
B1: A's component perpendicular to the line of centres is unchanged at 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m s⁻¹
M1: momentum along the line of centres: 2m(5 cos 30°) = 2m v_A + m v_B
M1: Newton's law of restitution: v_B − v_A = ½ × 5 cos 30°
A1: v_A = 5√3/4 = 2.17 m s⁻¹ along the line of centres, v_B = 5√3/2 = 4.33 m s⁻¹
A1: speed of A = √(2.165² + 2.5²) = 3.31 m s⁻¹
A1: A moves at 49.1° to the line of centres

long.q: A smooth sphere moving on a smooth horizontal floor strikes a fixed smooth vertical wall, approaching at 45° to the wall and rebounding at 30° to the wall. Find the coefficient of restitution, and the fraction of the sphere's kinetic energy lost in the impact.
scheme: M1: parallel component u cos 45° is unchanged
M1: perpendicular component becomes e u sin 45°
M1: tan 30° = e u sin 45° ÷ u cos 45° = e tan 45°
M1: KE after ÷ KE before = cos²45° + e² sin²45° = ½ + 1/6

long.q: A smooth sphere A moving with speed u collides with an identical smooth sphere B at rest. At impact the direction of motion of A makes an angle α (0 < α < 90°) with the line of centres. The collision is perfectly elastic. Show that after the collision the spheres move at right angles to each other.
scheme: M1: conservation of momentum along the line of centres: u cos α = v_A + v_B
M1: restitution with e = 1: v_B − v_A = u cos α
A1: v_A = 0 and v_B = u cos α along the line of centres
B1: perpendicular to the line of centres A keeps u sin α and B has 0
A1: A moves perpendicular to the line of centres and B along it, so their paths are at right angles

long.q: Two smooth spheres A and B of equal radius have masses 2 kg and 3 kg and move on a smooth horizontal plane. Just before they collide, A has velocity (4i + 3j) m s⁻¹ and B has velocity (−2i + j) m s⁻¹, and their line of centres is parallel to i. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find the velocities of A and B after the collision and the loss of kinetic energy.
scheme: B1: the j-components (3 and 1) are unchanged
M1: restitution along i: v_B − v_A = 0.5(4 − (−2)) = 3
M1: KE before 32.5 J, KE after 10.96 + 5.34 = 16.3 J

questions.why: G(y) = P(X² ≤ y) = P(X ≤ √y) = F(√y) = y/4, and y runs from 0 to 2² = 4.

long.q: The continuous random variable X has probability density function f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and f(x) = 0 otherwise. Find k, E(X) and Var(X), and the median of X.
scheme: M1: E(X) = ∫ x³/9 dx and E(X²) = ∫ x⁴/9 dx over 0 to 3

long.q: The cumulative distribution function of X is F(x) = 0 for x < 1, F(x) = (x² − 1)/8 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, and F(x) = 1 for x > 3. Find the probability density function of X, P(X > 2), and the upper quartile of X.
scheme: A1: f(x) = x/4 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 otherwise

long.q: The random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 3x²/8 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 otherwise. Y = X³. Find the probability density function of Y, and hence E(Y).
scheme: A1: g(y) = 1/8 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 8 and 0 otherwise (Y is uniform)

long.q: The random variable X has probability density function f(x) = k/x² for 1 ≤ x ≤ 4 and 0 otherwise. Find k, E(X) and the median of X, and comment on the skewness of the distribution.
scheme: A1: median 1.6, which is less than the mean, so the distribution is positively skewed

long.q: The random variable X has probability density function f(x) = ¾(1 − x²) for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 otherwise. Find E(X), Var(X) and Var(3X + 2).

M1: E(X²) = ∫ ¾(x² − x⁴) dx from −1 to 1

o: σ is unknown and the sample is small
questions.why: With σ estimated from a small sample, the t-distribution applies.

questions.q: Which conclusion to a hypothesis test is acceptable?
o: There is insufficient evidence to support the claim
questions.why: Examiners (2023): conclusions should include uncertainty, not 'the test proves that…'.

questions.q: A small sample comes from a normal population with unknown variance. Which distribution is used for the mean?
o: t with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Chi-squared with n degrees of freedom
questions.why: Examiners (2023): an incorrect t-value was the most common error.

questions.q: A random sample of 10 from a normal population has mean 52.3 and unbiased variance estimate 6.4. What is the test statistic for H₀: μ = 50?
questions.why: t = (52.3 − 50)/√(6.4/10) = 2.3/0.8 = 2.875, compared with t on 9 degrees of freedom.

questions.q: A pooled two-sample t-test compares samples of sizes 6 and 9 from normal populations with a common variance. How many degrees of freedom does the t-distribution have?
questions.why: The pooled variance estimate loses one degree of freedom per sample mean: ν = 6 + 9 − 2 = 13.

long.q: The lengths, x mm, of a random sample of 10 bolts from a machine are summarised by Σx = 512 and Σx² = 26 285. Assuming lengths are normally distributed, test at the 5% significance level whether the mean length is greater than 50 mm.
scheme: A1: 1.35 < 1.833 (t, 9 degrees of freedom), so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence that the mean length exceeds 50 mm

long.q: Eight students sat a test before and after a revision course. The differences d (after − before) in their scores give Σd = 20 and Σd² = 86. Assuming the differences are normally distributed, test at the 5% significance level whether the course increases the mean score.
scheme: B1: H₀: μ_d = 0, H₁: μ_d > 0, where μ_d is the population mean difference
A1: 3.12 > 1.895 (t, 7 degrees of freedom), so reject H₀: evidence that the course increases the mean score

long.q: The masses, in grams, of six randomly chosen apples are 11.8, 12.9, 13.5, 11.2, 12.6 and 12.4. Assuming the masses are normally distributed, find a 95% confidence interval for the population mean mass.
scheme: M1: unbiased estimate of variance Σ(x − x̄)²/5
M1: x̄ ± t s/√6 with t = 2.571 (5 degrees of freedom)

long.q: Independent random samples from two populations give: sample A, n = 8, mean 24.5, unbiased variance estimate 4.2; sample B, n = 10, mean 22.6, unbiased variance estimate 3.6. Stating any assumptions you make, test at the 5% significance level whether the two population means differ.
scheme: B1: H₀: μ_A = μ_B, H₁: μ_A ≠ μ_B
B1: assume both populations are normal with a common variance
B1: critical value 2.120 (16 degrees of freedom, two-tailed)
A1: 2.04 < 2.120, so do not reject H₀: insufficient evidence that the means differ

long.q: A random sample of 60 values from population 1 has mean 72.3 and unbiased variance estimate 25. An independent random sample of 50 values from population 2 has mean 69.8 and unbiased variance estimate 30. Find a 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂, and explain why it is not necessary to assume that the populations are normally distributed.
scheme: B1: the samples are large, so by the central limit theorem the sample means are approximately normally distributed

In a contingency table with grand total 100, a cell's row total is 40 and its column total is 30. What is its expected frequency under independence?
questions.why: Expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total = 40 × 30/100 = 12.

questions.q: A cell has observed frequency 18 and expected frequency 12. What does it contribute to the χ² statistic?
questions.why: (O − E)²/E = 6²/12 = 3. Dividing by O instead of E gives 2.

long.q: In a χ² goodness-of-fit test with 5 classes, the expected frequencies come from a distribution whose mean was estimated from the data. State the number of degrees of freedom and why.
scheme: B1: one is lost because totals agree, one because a parameter (the mean) was estimated

long.q: A random sample of 150 people were asked which of three sports, A, B or C, they preferred. Of 70 males, 30 chose A, 25 chose B and 15 chose C; of 80 females, 20 chose A, 35 chose B and 25 chose C. Test at the 5% significance level whether preferred sport is independent of gender.
scheme: B1: H₀: preference is independent of gender; H₁: they are not independent
M1: expected frequency = row total × column total ÷ 150
B1: 2 degrees of freedom, critical value 5.991
A1: 5.52 < 5.991, so do not reject H₀: no significant evidence of association

long.q: The numbers of calls received by a help desk on 200 days were: 0 calls on 30 days, 1 on 62, 2 on 56, 3 on 32, 4 on 14, and 5 or more on 6. Test at the 5% significance level whether the data are consistent with a Poisson distribution with mean 1.8.
scheme: B1: H₀: the number of calls follows Po(1.8); H₁: it does not
M1: expected frequencies 200 × P(X = r) from Po(1.8), with the last class 200 × P(X ≥ 5)
A1: 5 degrees of freedom (no parameter estimated), 0.740 < 11.07, so do not reject H₀: the data fit Po(1.8)

long.q: A genetic theory predicts that four types of plant occur in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. In a sample of 160 plants the observed frequencies were 97, 28, 26 and 9. Test at the 5% significance level whether the data are consistent with the theory.
scheme: M1: expected frequencies in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 out of 160
A1: 3 degrees of freedom, 1.31 < 7.815, so do not reject H₀: data consistent with the theory

long.q: In a goodness-of-fit test for a binomial distribution, the parameter p was estimated from the data. There are 7 classes, and the expected frequencies of the last three classes are 6.2, 3.1 and 1.4. Explain what should be done before calculating the test statistic, and state the number of degrees of freedom.
scheme: B1: expected frequencies below 5 make the χ² approximation unreliable
M1: combine the last two classes: 3.1 + 1.4 = 4.5, still below 5
A1: so combine the last three classes (total 10.7), leaving 5 classes

questions.q: In a sign test there are 10 non-zero differences, 8 of them positive. Testing for a positive median difference, what is P(X ≥ 8) when X ~ B(10, 0.5)?
questions.why: P(X ≥ 8) = (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 = 56/1024 ≈ 0.0547, which is not significant at the 5% level.

questions.q: Paired differences are 3, −1, 5, −2, 4. What is the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic T (the smaller rank sum)?
questions.why: Ranking |d|: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The negative differences have ranks 1 and 2, so T₋ = 3 and T₊ = 12; T = 3.

long.q: Twelve people rated a product before and after a demonstration. Nine ratings went up, two went down and one was unchanged. Use a sign test at the 5% significance level to test whether the demonstration tends to increase ratings.
scheme: B1: H₀: p = 0.5 (median difference 0); H₁: ratings tend to increase
B1: discard the unchanged rating, so n = 11
M1: number of decreases X ~ B(11, 0.5): P(X ≤ 2) = (1 + 11 + 55)/2048
A1: 0.0327 < 0.05, so reject H₀: evidence that ratings tend to increase

long.q: The following values are a random sample from a symmetric distribution: 23.1, 18.4, 25.6, 21.9, 19.5, 27.3, 24.2, 16.8, 22.7, 26.0. Use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the 5% significance level to test whether the population median is greater than 20.
scheme: M1: find the differences from 20 and rank their absolute values
A1: the negative differences −0.5, −1.6, −3.2 have ranks 1, 2 and 6
B1: critical value 10 for n = 10, one-tailed 5%
A1: 9 ≤ 10, so reject H₀: evidence that the median exceeds 20

long.q: Independent random samples of sizes 12 and 15 are taken from two populations. When all 27 values are ranked together, the ranks of the sample of size 12 sum to 210. Use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a normal approximation to test at the 5% significance level whether the two populations have the same median.
scheme: B1: H₀: the population medians are equal; H₁: they differ
M1: W = smaller of 210 and 12 × 28 − 210 = 126, compared with mean m(m + n + 1)/2
A1: z = −2.02; |z| > 1.96, so reject H₀: evidence that the medians differ

long.q: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test on a random sample of 30 paired differences gives T = 140. Use a normal approximation to test at the 5% significance level whether the population median difference is zero, against a two-sided alternative.
scheme: M1: mean n(n + 1)/4 and variance n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/24
A1: |z| < 1.96, so do not reject H₀: no significant evidence that the median difference is non-zero

long.q: Explain the circumstances in which a Wilcoxon signed-rank test would be used rather than a sign test, and rather than a t-test, when testing a hypothesis about a population average.
scheme: B1: the signed-rank test uses the sizes of the differences as well as their signs, so it is more powerful than the sign test
B1: it requires the population (of differences) to be symmetric; if it is not, the sign test should be used
B1: a t-test requires the population to be normally distributed
B1: so the signed-rank test is used when normality cannot be assumed (e.g. a small sample from an unknown distribution) but symmetry can
